1:
The heading detains the witnesses before a word of the prayer is heard, for "To the chief Musician upon Sheminith" yields them no settled sense. The reformed John Calvin owns two opinions and declines to fret over the choice: Sheminith is either a musical instrument or a tune, and the guess that it opened some familiar song seems to him less likely than that it names the air to which the psalm was to be sung. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reaches further, recording the Arabic title — "concerning the end of the world on the eighth day, a prophecy relative to the advent of the Messiah" — while himself judging the psalm most likely written during the Babylonish captivity. The latin-fathers Augustine of Hippo takes "the eighth" mystically, as the day of judgment or the eternal age given to the saints once the seven-day cycle of this present time is past.

When the cry itself breaks in — "help, LORD; for the godly man ceaseth" — the reformed John Gill reads the godly man by the notation of the word, one who has received grace and mercy and is beneficent, kind, and merciful; such may be said to cease when their number is greatly reduced, whether by death or by men once thought godly proving otherwise. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the philology: the sigh hoshiah carries its object within itself, work deliverance; gamar here means to have an end, as at Ps. 7:9, and the rare pasas to come to the extremity, to cease; the chasid is he who practises mercy, the amun the reliable, faithful, conscientious man, literally one who is firm.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in it the note of bad times, when there is a general decay of piety and honesty; the godly and the faithful are set together, for godly men are faithful men, "fast men," whose word is as binding as their bond, and they are taken away by death or desertion till scarcely an Israelite indeed can be found — though Henry hopes David erred, as Elijah did who thought himself left alone when God had seven thousand (Rom. 11:3). Here the witnesses divide over one word: the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the Vulgate and Syriac treat "the faithful" as an abstract, "truth" or "faithfulness," yet the parallelism (Ps. 31:23) requires the concrete, the Hebrew being cognate with "amen," so that Luther rendered it "amen’s leute," people as good as their word. Charles Spurgeon adds that "Help, Lord" is a short prayer, an angel’s sword to be turned every way, and that the decline of the godly should be a trumpet-call to more prayer.
2:
The badness of the age is now traced to its tongue, and the witnesses take up the double-dealing speech that fills it. Where the psalm charges that "they speak vanity every one with his neighbour," the reformed John Gill reads the vanity as that which is false and a lie, whether in doctrine or in practice, vain and empty, frothy and corrupt, the kind of thing no godly or faithful man would utter; and its being done in common, by the generality of men one with another, only shows how far the degeneracy already bewailed has spread. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears men false and hollow, who say one thing while they mean another, so that there is no trusting what they say; and he fastens on the Hebrew of the second clause, beleb valeb, "with a heart and a heart," as though such men were furnished with two hearts, one to speak the fair words and the other to invent the mischief beneath them.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sees dissimulation and flattery corrupting all converse: men grown so profligate that they make no conscience of a lie, yet so base as to cover the worst designs with the most specious professions of friendship, so that they "speak vanity every one with his neighbour" and will kiss and kill at once, as Joab did Abner and Amasa in David’s own day, smiling in the face and cutting the throat — the devil’s image complete, a complication of malice and falsehood. The times are bad indeed, Henry adds, when there is no sincerity to be met with, and an honest man knows not whom to believe, nor whom to trust, nor dares put confidence in a friend or a guide.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the figure from the very letter of the text. "Vanity," he observes, is literally "evil," and "falsehood" would render it better (compare Ps. 41:6); the words may even have lain in Paul’s mind when he bade the Ephesians speak every man truth with his neighbour (Eph. 4:25). "Flattering lips" he renders literally "lips of smoothness," as at Ps. 5:9, and "a double heart" literally "a heart and a heart," as in 1 Chron. 12:33; and over the whole he hangs the mordant sentence of the old preacher Thomas Adams, who turned the doubled heart into a portrait of his age — one for the Church, another for the Change, one for Sundays, another for working-days — and concluded, "a man without a heart is a wonder, but a man with two hearts is a monster." The witnesses do not divide over the sin: whether it be named vanity, evil, or falsehood, all hear in it the speech of a heart doubled upon itself, fair in the mouth and foul beneath.
3:
What the flatterers have set in motion, the psalm now turns over to God, and the witnesses ask in what mood the turning is made. The reformed John Gill notes at once that "the LORD shall cut off all flattering lips" may be read either as a prophecy or as a prayer, as Aben Ezra and Kimchi observe; God will cut off the deceitful, whether by some judgment in this life or by everlasting punishment hereafter, taking them away by death "out of the world," as the Targum turns it, or casting them into the hell where all liars have their portion. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott comes down for the second mood, translating the clause as petition — "may Jehovah cut off" — and glossing "proud things" as literally "great things," the Vulgate’s linguam magniloquam, the great swelling tongue. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees on the sense of the phrase, taking the gedoloth for the great swelling words such men use both in their promises and in their commendations, boasts as empty as they are loud.

The other grammatical-historical voice, Keil and Delitzsch, reads the verb as a true voluntative with its own proper force — "may He root out" — and sets the wish over against the security of the boasters, comparing the like prayer of Ps. 109:15 and its opposite at Ps. 11:6. So a real difference runs beneath the line: whether David foretells, in calm assurance, that God shall cut off the flattering lips, or prays, in the heat of his grievance, that God may. The witnesses do not treat the two as enemies, for Gill will have it a prophecy and a prayer at once; yet the grammarians lean to the petition, hearing a wish rather than a promise.

The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon feels the certainty of the doom whichever way the verb be pointed: total destruction shall overwhelm the lovers of flattery and pride, whom the apostle called "raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame." And he marks the justice of classing the two sins together, the flattering lips and the tongue that speaks proud things, for they are one vice under two faces — the first flatters another and the second flatters himself, and in both a lie is in the right hand. None, Spurgeon adds, are so detestably domineering as the little creatures who creep into office by cringing to the great, so that even in the lowest meanness there is no small degree of pride. The witnesses agree that the loud tongue and the smooth one shall be silenced together, and that the God who is flattered by neither will cut off both.
4:
The proud speech of the age now comes to its head in a boast of sheer independence, and the witnesses listen to men who own no master over their mouths. The reformed John Gill reads "with our tongue will we prevail" of men confident that, whether through the eloquence or the outward power that backs them, their word shall stand as law and none withstand it; and he turns the clause toward antichrist, "we will make one to prevail," the man of sin whose edicts have obtained everywhere. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the second clause, "our lips are our own": many think that because they have the faculty of speech they may therefore speak whatever they please, worshipping their own tongue as though its eloquence were their own and owed nothing to God. John Wesley glosses the prevailing as the raising and spreading of evil reports, and "our own" as lips at their own disposal to say what they will — "who can control or restrain us?"

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears in the boast the voice of men who have the ear of those in authority and can "make the worse appear the better cause," or who, being themselves in high place, defy their victims as Angelo defies Isabel in the play, "who will believe thee?" But he owns a great difference of opinion over the rendering: whether "with our tongues will we prevail," or "we are masters of our tongues," or "with our tongues we confederate," our tongues being our allies — the last, he thinks, agreeing best with what follows, "our lips are with us," that is, upon our side. Keil and Delitzsch reason to the same end from the grammar, weighing the Hiphil higbir — to impart strength, or to give proof of it — and preferring, from its construction, "we will give emphasis to our tongue," the self-assured declaration of men who make their very lips their confederates and ask, "who is lord over us?"

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into the portrait of a proud impiety. Such men have arrived at a pitch where they fancy the point gained by eating forbidden fruit, that they are as gods, self-sufficient and infallible, able like God himself to speak and have it done; and their "our lips are our own" he calls an unjust pretension, "for who made man’s mouth, in whose hand is his breath, and whose is the air he breathes in?" Their "who is lord over us?" is the very language of Pharaoh (Exod. 5:1), as absurd as it is insolent, for he in whom we live and move and have our being must needs be, by an indisputable title, Lord over us. The witnesses do not divide: whether the tongue be their weapon or their ally, the sin is the same, the creature’s mad claim to be lord of his own words and answerable to none.
5:
Against the boasters God himself now speaks, and the witnesses hear the divine answer to the whole complaint. The reformed John Gill takes the oppressed poor for the servants and people of God, poor often in estate and always in spirit, afflicted and despised and trodden down by the insolent men just described, as Israel was oppressed by Egypt. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke refers the oppression to the captive Israelites in Babylon, over whom the Lord represents himself as looking on, seeing their affliction and hearing their cry, until he rises to their help: "now will I arise" — I alone gave them into their enemies’ hands for their transgressions, and I alone will deliver them, that the manner of it may show the power of their God.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the verse as an ancient oracle of God, quoted here and then set, in the next line, against the false speeches of hypocrites, the true and genuine word of God contrasted with their alloy. Keil and Delitzsch fix the movement of it precisely: the two prepositions name the motive, the "now" the decisive turn from forbearance to the execution of judgment, and the verb the divine determination that has just made itself audible, echoed, they note, by Isaiah’s "now will I arise" (Isa. 33:10).

Here the witnesses part over the last clause. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads "him that puffeth at him" of the proud oppressor who despises the poor man and hopes to destroy him with a puff of breath, and Gill and Clarke keep the same sense of scornful contempt, Clarke owning that the words are hard and that several versions escape the difficulty with "I will give him an open salvation." But the grammatical-historical voices turn the panting the other way. Ellicott renders it "I will set in safety him that panteth for it," ensuring him the safety for which he longs, and Keil and Delitzsch expressly reject "him whom the boaster blows upon" in favour of "him who longs for" deliverance, both fixing the sense by Hab. 2:3, where the same verb means to pant after a thing’s accomplishment. So the "puffing" is read two ways: the sneer of the oppressor who blows upon his victim, or the yearning of the oppressed who pants for the rescue God now promises. Charles Spurgeon, hearing the verse as a whole, finds the very oppression of the saints to be a cry that moves God as a father is moved by his children’s tears, so that Moses was heard at the Red Sea though he said nothing, and the needy who dare only sigh in secret are heard and set on high above their tormentor’s rage.
6:
"The words of the LORD are pure words," and the witnesses set the divine speech against every human tongue in the psalm. The reformed John Gill hears the observation made in direct opposition to the deceitful words of the wicked: the Scriptures, the promises, the Gospel are all the words of God, pure and holy, free from all human mixture and from all fraud and deceit, the very Scriptures of truth. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon draws the same contrast to a point — man’s words are yea and nay, but the Lord’s promises yea and amen — and pushes the figure of the furnace into his own age: the Bible has passed through the fires of persecution, of literary criticism, of philosophic doubt, and of scientific discovery, and has lost nothing but those human interpretations that clung to it as alloy clings to precious ore.

The figure of the refining the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke expounds with a metallurgist’s care, taking the "furnace of earth" for the cupel by which silver is purified: the metal, mingled with lead and laid in a vessel of calcined bone, is exposed to a fierce heat until its impurities are absorbed or thrown off in fume, and it continues in agitation until, all dross gone, it lies perfectly still — the very token, he says, that answers to the "seven times," a perfect purification. John Wesley keeps the plain doctrine, that the words are pure, without the least mixture of falsehood, and therefore shall infallibly be fulfilled.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott labours over the difficult phrase "of earth." It must mean, he judges, either "in earth," of the ashes into which the smelted silver falls, or "as to earth," that is, purified of the alloy; yet he notes that the Hebrew erets is nowhere else used for the material earth, and reports Hitzig’s emendation, rats, a bar or piece (Ps. 68:30), yielding "melted into a bar from the crucible," a change he finds almost convincing in its simplicity and aptness. Keil and Delitzsch turn from the crucible to the comfort, hearing in the pure words the ground of the consolatory hope that rises in the psalm, the divine utterance on which the next verse will build its confidence. The witnesses do not divide over the sum of it: in a world where every neighbour speaks vanity, the one speech that is tried and untainted is the word of the Lord, silver seven times refined, on which the oppressed may stake all they cannot stake on men.
7:
The promise of the pure words carries at once into a promise of preservation, and here the witnesses divide over the plainest of questions: whom, or what, will God keep? The reformed John Gill argues from the grammar that "thou shalt keep them" cannot mean the words, as Aben Ezra held, since the affix is masculine and not feminine; the sense, as Kimchi rightly saw, is that God will keep the poor and needy whom he has just set in safety, for they are not their own keepers but are kept by his power and in his Son, preserved from a total and final falling away. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch reason to the same conclusion from the suffixes: the first refers to the miserable and poor, and the second, being "him" and not "us," reaches back to the very man who yearned for deliverance in the oracle, so that the preserving is so constant that neither now nor at any time to come will he succumb to this generation.

Against this stands the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley, who reads "thou shalt keep them" of God’s words or promises: these he will observe and keep, both now and from this generation for ever, so that the verse becomes a pledge of the endurance of the very words just called pure. So the debate is real and turns on a single pronoun: whether it is the tried words of God that are kept unbroken through every faithless age, or the tried people of God who are kept unfallen in the midst of it. Gill will allow that God has wonderfully preserved the sacred writings and keeps every word of promise, yet insists the pronoun here points to the persons, not the promises.

The other wesleyan-arminian voice, Adam Clarke, brings a textual variant to the same verse, noting that several manuscripts, with the Septuagint, the Vulgate, and the Arabic, read not "them" but "us" — "thou shalt keep us, thou shalt preserve us" — the sense, he thinks, equally good either way; and he reads the preserving historically, of the God who brought Israel out of Babylon according to his word and has kept them, generation after generation, a distinct people to this day. Whether the kept be the words or the poor, the promises or the persons, and whether the text say "them" or "us," the witnesses agree on the substance of the comfort: that in a generation of proud and lying men there is a keeping power not their own, under which what God has spoken and whom God has chosen are alike secured against the age that would wear them out. It is the same assurance, Keil and Delitzsch add, that the oppression shall not deepen into ruin, nor the trial exceed the power to endure it.
8:
The psalm closes where it began, in a world overrun, and the witnesses gather at a last verse whose very words they cannot agree to read. The reformed John Gill takes "the wicked walk on every side" of the poor and righteous, whom they compass about to watch, to snare, and to hurt, for the whole world lies in wickedness and its men, like their father the devil, go about to do all the mischief they can, so that the saints stand in continual need of the divine preservation just promised. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry ties the wickedness to the rulers who countenance it: when the vilest men are exalted to places of trust and power, and instead of executing the laws against vice protect and patronise it, then the wicked walk on every side and swarm in all places, neither afraid nor ashamed, declaring their sin as Sodom with none to check them; for when the wicked bear rule, the people mourn.

Charles Spurgeon, the other puritan-evangelical voice, draws the same moral and turns it to hope: when those in power are vile their underlings will be no better, as a warm sun brings out noxious flies, yet the glory and triumph of the exalted Redeemer should the more embolden his saints to walk and work on every side, meeting the evils of the time with holy resolution and the old prayer, "Help, Lord." John Wesley reads the walking plainly, of wicked men who fill all places and go about boldly and securely.

But over the wording the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott open a real question. Clarke would render the second clause not "when the vilest men are exalted" but "as villany gains ground among the sons of Adam," following the Vulgate’s turn of the Hebrew; while Ellicott reports Gesenius’s version, "the wicked walk on every side like the rising of a tempest upon the sons of men," and, comparing kindred passages (Ps. 39:6), offers his own, "the wicked vanish on every side," at the rising of a tempest upon the sons of men. So the last line is read three ways — of vile men lifted into office, of vileness itself spreading through the race, or of the wicked swept off like a passing storm. The witnesses do not divide over the burden of the psalm, which all take to be the triumph of God’s keeping over a faithless generation; they part only over whether its final word paints the wicked enthroned, the wickedness rising, or the wicked at last blown away. And they close, with Spurgeon, on the note the psalm began with, the cry "Help, Lord," now answered by the God whose pure words preserve his own for ever.
